content: Medroxyprogesterone injection can lead to a reduction in the calcium content of your bones. The longer you use this medication, the greater the potential decrease in bone calcium. Even after discontinuing medroxyprogesterone, the calcium levels in your bones may not return to normal. This loss of calcium can result in osteoporosis, a condition characterized by weakened and brittle bones, and may increase the likelihood of bone fractures later in life, particularly after menopause. Bone calcium typically increases during adolescence, a critical period for bone strengthening, and any reduction in calcium during this time can have serious consequences. It is unclear whether starting medroxyprogesterone injections during adolescence or early adulthood increases the risk of developing osteoporosis later in life. Inform your doctor if you or a family member has osteoporosis, a history of bone disease, or anorexia nervosa (an eating disorder). Additionally, disclose if you consume large amounts of alcohol or smoke heavily. Notify your doctor if you are taking medications such as corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone, methylprednisolone, prednisone) or seizure medications (e.g., carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital). Medroxyprogesterone injection should not be used for more than two years unless no other birth control method or treatment option is suitable for your condition. Your doctor may perform bone density tests to ensure your bones are not becoming too thin before continuing this medication. Attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and laboratory to monitor your health and prevent osteoporosis. Discuss the risks of using medroxyprogesterone injection with your doctor. Medroxyprogesterone injection is prescribed to prevent pregnancy. It is available as an intramuscular injection (into a muscle) or a subcutaneous injection (under the skin). The medication works by preventing ovulation (the release of eggs from the ovaries), thereby preventing pregnancy. In women with endometriosis, it also slows the spread of uterine tissue to other parts of the body. While medroxyprogesterone injection is a highly effective birth control method, it does not protect against the transmission of HIV or other sexually transmitted infections. The intramuscular injection is administered as a liquid into the buttocks or upper arm, typically once every three months (13 weeks) by a healthcare provider in a clinical setting. The subcutaneous injection is administered just under the skin, usually every 12–14 weeks, also by a healthcare provider. The first injection must be given at a time when pregnancy is not possible, such as during the first five days of a normal menstrual period, within five days after childbirth if not breastfeeding, or during the sixth week postpartum if breastfeeding. If switching from another birth control method, your doctor will advise when to receive your first injection. Before using medroxyprogesterone injection, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to medroxyprogesterone or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Mention any medications listed in the Important Warning section, as well as aminoglutethimide. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. Inform your doctor if you or a family member has a history of breast cancer or diabetes. Also, disclose any history of breast issues (e.g., lumps, nipple bleeding, abnormal mammograms, fibrocystic breast disease), unexplained vaginal bleeding, irregular or light menstrual periods, excessive weight gain or fluid retention before periods, blood clots, stroke, migraines, seizures, depression, high blood pressure, heart attack, asthma, or liver, kidney, or heart disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or think you might be pregnant, inform your doctor immediately. Medroxyprogesterone may harm the fetus. If you are breastfeeding, you may use medroxyprogesterone injection as long as your baby is at least six weeks old when you receive your first injection. Some medroxyprogesterone may pass into breast milk, but studies have not shown harm to breastfed babies. Inform your doctor or dentist that you are using medroxyprogesterone injection if you are undergoing surgery, including dental procedures. Be aware that your menstrual cycle will likely change while using medroxyprogesterone injection. Initially, your periods may become irregular, and you may experience spotting between periods. Continued use may result in the complete cessation of periods. Your menstrual cycle will likely return to normal after discontinuing the medication. While using medroxyprogesterone injection, consume foods rich in calcium and vitamin D to minimize bone calcium loss. Your doctor will recommend appropriate foods and the number of servings you need daily. Calcium or vitamin D supplements may also be prescribed or recommended. If you miss an appointment for your medroxyprogesterone injection, contact your doctor. Missing an injection may reduce your protection against pregnancy. Your doctor will advise when to receive the missed injection and may administer a pregnancy test to ensure you are not pregnant before giving the injection. Use an alternative birth control method, such as condoms, until you receive the missed injection. Medroxyprogesterone injection may cause side effects. Notify your doctor if you experience any of the following symptoms, especially if they are severe or persistent: changes in menstrual periods, weight gain, weakness, fatigue, nervousness, irritability, depression, difficulty sleeping, hot flashes, breast pain or tenderness, stomach cramps, leg cramps, back or joint pain, acne, hair loss, vaginal irritation or discharge, changes in sexual desire, cold or flu symptoms, or injection site reactions (e.g., pain, redness, swelling). Serious side effects are rare but require immediate medical attention. These include sudden shortness of breath, sharp chest pain, coughing up blood, severe headache, vomiting, dizziness, vision changes, difficulty speaking, limb weakness or numbness, seizures, yellowing of the skin or eyes, leg swelling or tenderness, heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding, severe pelvic pain, rash, hives, difficulty breathing, or signs of infection at the injection site. If you are under 35 and began using medroxyprogesterone injection in the last 4–5 years, you may have a slightly increased risk of breast cancer. This medication may also increase the risk of blood clots in the lungs or brain. Discuss these risks with your doctor. Medroxyprogesterone injection is a long-acting birth control method, and fertility may take time to return after the last injection. If you plan to become pregnant soon, discuss the potential effects of this medication with your doctor. Report any unusual problems while using this medication to your doctor. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA MedWatch program. Your doctor will store this medication in their office. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call 911 if the individual collapses or is not breathing. You should have a complete physical exam, including blood pressure measurements, breast and pelvic exams, and a Pap test, at least annually. Follow your doctor’s instructions for breast self-exams and report any lumps immediately. Inform laboratory personnel that you are using medroxyprogesterone before undergoing any tests.
